posts.title: Dizzy on rolling over: test for BPPV
posts.insight: Positional dizziness in older people has a named test (Dix-Hallpike) and a treatment (a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley) that resolves it in about 56 in 100 people, against 21 in 100 without it.
posts.angle: Ask about positional triggers and examine before reaching for a vague label or a sedating anti-dizziness tablet. Position: BPPV should be looked for in older people with dizziness.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the guideline recommendations and trial figures are empirical and guideline content; 'look for it before labelling' is clinical interpretation.

captions.x:
Dizziness that starts when an older person rolls over in bed, looks up or bends down has a specific test and a specific treatment.

The US ENT guideline (AAO-HNS 2017) strongly recommends the Dix-Hallpike test for the commonest type of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), and a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley. It advises against routine sedating anti-dizziness medicines, such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines.

In trials, about 56 in 100 people were free of vertigo after the Epley, against 21 in 100 after a sham or nothing. About a third had it come back.

Ask what brings the dizziness on. Then examine.
captions.linkedin:
Dizziness that starts when an older person rolls over in bed, looks up or bends down has a specific test and a specific treatment.

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is brief spinning brought on by head position. In one US study at an inner-city clinic for older people, about 9 in 100 patients had BPPV that nobody had recognised. Those with it were more likely to have fallen in the previous three months. A single snapshot study from one clinic can't show that BPPV caused the falls, and the figure is not a general prevalence.

The US ENT guideline (AAO-HNS 2017):

1. Strongly recommends diagnosing the commonest type with the Dix-Hallpike test.
2. Strongly recommends treating it with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley.
3. Advises against routinely treating BPPV with sedating anti-dizziness medicines, such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines.
4. Asks clinicians to assess falls risk and mobility.

The Cochrane review of the Epley manoeuvre found complete resolution of vertigo in about 56 in 100 people, against about 21 in 100 after a sham manoeuvre or no treatment. BPPV often came back, in about a third. Some people with neck problems could not tolerate the manoeuvre. The trials were mostly small, with short follow up, and were not specific to frail older people.

So the first question for an older person with dizziness is what brings it on. If the answer is lying down, rolling over or looking up, examine for BPPV before the dizziness gets a general label or a sedating tablet.

More Teaching round posts take one bedside test or clinical distinction at a time.

posts.title: Sudden hearing loss in one ear: get it checked urgently
posts.insight: Sudden hearing loss in one ear should be checked urgently, because a clinician needs to tell a blocked ear canal from inner-ear or nerve loss, and any steroid treatment is time-limited.
posts.angle: Do not assume wax. Ask for an urgent check and ask which kind of loss it is.
posts.position_basis: mixed: urgency and the two kinds of loss are guideline content (AAO-HNS 2019); the uncertain steroid benefit is empirical (Cochrane); 'ask for an urgent appointment' is practical advice.

captions.x:
Hearing gone in one ear, suddenly, over a day or overnight: this needs an urgent check.

It is easy to assume wax and reach for drops. The US ENT guideline says a clinician first needs to tell whether the ear canal is blocked or whether the inner ear or the nerve is affected.

The difference changes what happens next. Steroid treatment is an option if it starts within about two weeks, though trials have not shown clearly that it works.

Ask for an urgent appointment, and ask: is my ear blocked, or is this the inner ear?
captions.linkedin:
Hearing gone in one ear, suddenly, over a day or overnight: this needs an urgent check.

It is easy to assume the cause is wax, buy drops and wait. The trouble is that two quite different problems can feel the same to the person.

One is a blocked ear canal, for example with wax. The other is a problem in the inner ear or the hearing nerve, called sudden sensorineural hearing loss.

The US ENT guideline (AAO-HNS 2019) says sudden hearing loss should be checked urgently, and that the first job is to tell these two apart.

The reason for hurry is the treatment window. The guideline lists steroid treatment as an option if it starts within about two weeks. Cochrane reviews of steroid tablets and of steroid injections into the ear have not shown clearly that they work, so this is an option to discuss rather than a sure fix. That uncertainty is a reason to decide early, while there is still a choice to make.

If this happens to you or to someone you care for, ask for an urgent appointment rather than waiting to see if it clears. Then ask one question: is the ear canal blocked, or is this the inner ear?

posts.title: Seeing things after sight loss
posts.insight: People losing their sight can see vivid images they know are not real (Charles Bonnet syndrome); it is often kept secret for fear of being thought mentally ill, and a correct explanation helps.
posts.angle: Name the condition so people can mention it; new hallucinations still need checking for other causes. Position: eye clinics should mention it at diagnosis (judgement).
posts.position_basis: mixed: description, Dutch study figures and fear of disclosure are empirical; 'we should tell people at diagnosis' is ethical and clinical judgement.

captions.x:
Some people losing their sight start to see vivid images that are not there: patterns, flowers, faces. They know the images are not real.

This is Charles Bonnet syndrome, most often seen with macular degeneration.

In a Dutch clinic study of 505 people with sight loss, 60 had these images. Of 16 who had seen a doctor about them, only 1 got the right explanation. All were glad to hear it was not mental illness.

If this happens to you, mention it to your doctor. New images still need checking for other causes. We should tell people about it when sight loss is diagnosed.
captions.linkedin:
Some people losing their sight start to see vivid images that are not there: patterns, flowers, faces. They know the images are not real.

This is called Charles Bonnet syndrome. It is seen most often in people with macular degeneration, the condition that affects the centre of vision.

Many people keep the images to themselves, for fear of being thought mentally ill.

A Dutch study published in 1996 looked at 505 people attending a clinic with sight loss. 60 had these images. Every one of them knew the images were not real. Of 16 who had seen a doctor about them, only 1 had been given the right explanation. All were glad to hear it was not mental illness.

That is one clinic, nearly 30 years ago, so the figures should not be read as how common it is today, and awareness may have improved. The fear of speaking up is still described in recent reviews.

Two things follow. New hallucinations should still be mentioned to a doctor, because other causes need to be ruled out. And explaining the condition is a large part of the help.

Our view: people should be told about Charles Bonnet syndrome when sight loss is diagnosed, before the images start, so they are not left wondering what is happening to their mind.

posts.title: Hearing near the end of life
posts.insight: In 5 hospice patients who had stopped responding, the brain still reacted to changes in tones; this shows sound was still being processed, not that words were understood.
posts.angle: Speak to a dying person as someone who may hear, while being honest about how small and limited the evidence is.
posts.position_basis: mixed: brain responses in 5 of 5 and 2 of 5 are empirical; that the result lends some support to talking to a dying relative is the authors' interpretation; 'we should keep talking' is judgement.

captions.x:
In a Vancouver hospice, researchers recorded brain activity in 5 people who had stopped responding and were close to death.

All 5 showed brain responses to changes in simple tones. 2 showed a response that, in healthy people, goes with consciously noticing the change.

That shows the ear and brain were still reacting to sound. It does not show that anyone understood words or knew who was there. It is one small study.

The authors say it lends some support to talking to a dying relative. We think that is reason enough: keep speaking to them as someone who may hear.
captions.linkedin:
In a Vancouver hospice, researchers recorded brain activity in 5 people who had stopped responding and were close to death.

They played patterns of simple tones and watched for the brain's electrical reaction when the pattern changed. All 5 showed brain responses to changes in the tones. 2 of the 5 showed a response that, in healthy people, goes with consciously noticing the change.

What this does show: the ear and the brain were still reacting to sound in people who could no longer respond.

What it does not show: that anyone understood words, recognised a voice, or knew who was in the room. The study used tones, not speech. The authors themselves say it is unclear how these responses relate to awareness, and one of them is thought to happen automatically.

It is also very small: 13 people recruited, 9 analysed, 5 recorded when unresponsive, mostly with cancer, compared with 17 young students.

The authors say the findings lend some support to the advice to keep talking to a dying relative. Our view is that the evidence is limited and the advice still stands on its own. Speaking to a dying person as someone who may hear costs nothing, and treats them as present.

If you are sitting with someone who is dying, say what you want to say. Tell them who is there.

Sources in the first comment.
captions.bluesky:
In 5 hospice patients who had stopped responding, the brain still reacted to changes in simple tones (2 of 5 in a way linked to noticing).

Tones, not words, and a tiny study.

Still, we think it is right to keep speaking to a dying person as someone who may hear.

posts.title: Loud enough, still unclear
posts.insight: Age-related hearing loss usually affects high-pitched sounds first, and many consonants are high-pitched, so a person can hear that someone is talking but miss parts of words. Louder does not restore the missing sounds.
posts.angle: Explain why 'I can hear you but not what you said' happens, and offer practical habits: attention first, face the person, speak clearly, try other words. These habits are practical advice, not trial findings.
posts.position_basis: mixed: high-pitch loss and consonants are empirical (Aydelott 2010); the communication habits are practical advice and judgement.

captions.x:
Many consonants, such as s, f and th, are high-pitched sounds. Age-related hearing loss usually takes high-pitched sounds first.

So a person can hear that you are talking, and still miss parts of the words. Saying it louder brings back the voice more than the missing sounds.

Practical habits that help, from experience of good communication rather than a trial: say their name first, sit facing them with your face in the light, speak clearly and a little slower, and if a word is missed, try different words.
captions.linkedin:
Many consonants, such as s, f and th, are high-pitched sounds. Age-related hearing loss usually takes high-pitched sounds first.

That explains a very common complaint: "I can hear you, I just can't make out what you said." The person hears the voice, which carries a lot of lower-pitched sound, but parts of the words go missing. Other changes in how the ageing brain processes speech add to this.

So repeating the same sentence louder often brings back more voice than meaning.

Practical habits that tend to help. These come from everyday good communication rather than from a trial:

1. Get their attention first. Say their name.
2. Face them, with your face in the light, so they can see your lips and expression.
3. Speak clearly and a little slower, at a normal volume.
4. If a word is missed, try different words rather than the same ones again.
5. Turn down the television or move away from the kitchen noise.

If the person has hearing aids, make sure they are in and working. None of this replaces a hearing test.

If you live with someone whose hearing is going, try one change this week: say their name before the sentence.

posts.title: Eye drops that slow the heart
posts.insight: Timolol eye drops are absorbed into the bloodstream and can act like a beta-blocker tablet; case reports describe severe bradycardia and heart block that resolved on stopping.
posts.angle: In an older person with bradycardia, syncope or falls, ask specifically about eye drops, which are often left off medicine lists, and discuss alternatives with the eye team.
posts.position_basis: mixed: systemic absorption and case reports are empirical (frequency unknown); 'ask about eye drops' is clinical interpretation.

captions.x:
Timolol eye drops reach the bloodstream and can act like a beta-blocker tablet.

Case reports describe very slow heart rates and heart block that settled when the drops were stopped. In one, the heart rate was 29 a minute, and it resolved within 48 hours of stopping, though the drops had unmasked an existing conduction problem. Case reports show it can happen, not how often.

In an older person with a slow pulse, blackouts or falls, ask about eye drops by name. If a beta-blocker drop may be responsible, other types of glaucoma drops exist: discuss with the eye team.
captions.linkedin:
Timolol eye drops reach the bloodstream and can act like a beta-blocker tablet.

A drop goes into the eye, drains through the tear duct into the nose, and is absorbed from there into the blood.

Case reports describe very slow heart rates and heart block that settled when the drops were stopped. In one report, a 62-year-old man on long-term timolol had a heart rate of 29 a minute with complete heart block, which resolved within 48 hours of stopping the drops. The drops had unmasked an existing problem in his heart's conduction system. Case reports show that this can happen; they do not tell us how often.

The teaching point is in the history. Eye drops are easy to leave off a medicine list, and people often do not think of them as medicines at all. In an older person with bradycardia, syncope, falls or new breathlessness, ask about eye drops by name.

Can absorption be reduced? In a small cross-over trial of 21 adults, pressing on the inner corner of the eye for 5 minutes after the drop, or pressing with a tissue, lowered the amount of timolol reaching the blood. That trial was not in older people and measured blood levels, not heart rate or falls, so clinical benefit is not shown.

If a beta-blocker drop may be responsible, other types of glaucoma drops exist. Discuss the options with the eye team rather than stopping treatment for glaucoma without a plan.

Sources in the first comment.

posts.title: The vision screening that did not improve vision
posts.insight: Trials of community vision screening in older people did not show better eyesight; the reviewers thought the likely reason was that treatment offered after screening was often not taken up.
posts.angle: A programme that counts problems found is not the same as one that corrects sight. Judge sight programmes by corrected sight, and make the step from detection to treatment easy.
posts.position_basis: mixed: null trial results are empirical; the take-up explanation is the reviewers' interpretation; 'judge programmes by corrected sight' is judgement.

captions.x:
Testing everyone's eyesight in a health check sounds like obvious good care for older people. In trials, it did not leave people seeing better.

A Cochrane review of 10 trials, over 10,000 people aged 65 and over living independently, found community vision screening did not improve eyesight. The reviewers thought the likely reason was that people often did not take up the treatment offered, while many unscreened people sought help themselves.

We should judge sight programmes by corrected sight, and make getting glasses or surgery after a test easy.
captions.linkedin:
Testing everyone's eyesight in a health check sounds like obvious good care for older people. In trials, it did not leave people seeing better.

In a UK trial in 20 general practices, 4,340 people aged 75 and over had either a vision test for everyone or a check that tested only some people. Three to five years later there was no clear difference in eyesight or in people's own rating of their vision. The comparison was with targeted testing, not with no testing.

A Cochrane review then pooled 10 trials with over 10,000 people aged 65 and over living independently. Community vision screening did not improve eyesight.

The reviewers' explanation, which is their interpretation rather than something the trials tested: people often did not take up the treatment offered after screening, while many unscreened people went and sought help themselves. They suggested testing approaches in more dependent people, who were largely outside these trials.

The trials tested screening, not the treatments themselves. Finding a problem is only the first step. Glasses, cataract surgery and low vision support help only if they reach the person.

Our view: sight programmes for older people should be judged by how many people end up seeing better, and should make the step from test to treatment easy: help with the appointment, the cost and the travel.

Sources in the first comment.

posts.title: Between the first and second cataract operation
posts.insight: After the first cataract operation, the two eyes can need very different glasses until the second eye is done; second-eye surgery evens this out and, in a trial of women over 70, improved sight and confidence.
posts.angle: The gap between operations is a real period of uneven sight. Ask about glasses before the first operation.
posts.position_basis: mixed: imbalance risk and trial results are empirical; 'ask before surgery' is practical advice.

captions.x:
Between the first and second cataract operation, your two eyes can need very different glasses.

The operated eye has changed; your old glasses were made for the eye it was before. In one Belfast waiting list, about 1 in 3 people waiting for their first eye were judged at risk of this troublesome imbalance.

Second-eye surgery evens it out. In a trial of 239 women over 70, having the second eye done within about a month rather than a year improved sight and confidence. Whether it reduced falls was uncertain.

Before the first operation, ask: what should I do about my glasses until the second eye is done?
captions.linkedin:
Between the first and second cataract operation, your two eyes can need very different glasses.

Cataract surgery replaces the cloudy lens inside the eye with a clear artificial one, and this usually changes the prescription for that eye. Your old glasses were made for both eyes as they were before. Until the second eye is done, one eye may be well corrected and the other not, and the glasses may suit neither.

How common is this? In one Belfast cataract waiting list in 2020, about 1 in 3 people waiting for their first eye were judged at risk of this troublesome imbalance after surgery. That was an estimate from one clinic, not a count of people with symptoms.

Second-eye surgery evens it out. In a Nottingham trial, 239 women over 70 were randomly assigned to have the second eye done within about a month or after the usual wait of around a year. Those operated sooner had better sight and more confidence. Whether it reduced falls was uncertain. The trial included only women.

The period between operations can last weeks or months, with stairs, kerbs and reading included.

If you are due to have a cataract operation, ask before the first eye is done: what should I do about my glasses until the second eye is done? Ask your optician too.

posts.title: Set up the cognitive test before you score it
posts.insight: People with hearing or sight loss pass the MoCA less often, even when scores are adjusted for items they could not hear or see; test administration should use aids and adaptations and record them with the score.
posts.angle: Practical test administration: hearing aids in, amplifier, glasses, large print, quiet room, and a note of the adaptations beside the score so the next reader can interpret it.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the Dupuis association is empirical; the administration checklist and recording adaptations are good-practice judgement.

captions.x:
Put the hearing aids in before the MoCA starts, and write down that you did.

In a Canadian study of 301 older adults, people with hearing or sight loss passed the MoCA less often, even after scores were adjusted for items they could not hear or see. That is an association: it could also reflect real differences in thinking.

So set the test up: hearing aids in and working, a personal amplifier if needed, the right glasses, large print, good light, a quiet room.

Then record the adaptations next to the score, so the next person reading it knows how it was done.
captions.linkedin:
Put the hearing aids in before the MoCA starts, and write down that you did.

The Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) depends on hearing spoken words and seeing drawings and print. In a Canadian study of 301 older adults, mean age 71, people with hearing or sight loss passed the MoCA less often than people without, even after scores were adjusted for items they could not hear or see.

That is an association. It may partly reflect real differences in thinking, and the study can't separate the two. What it does show is that a score from someone who could not hear or see the test well is hard to read.

A practical set-up, as good practice rather than a tested protocol:

1. Hearing aids in, switched on, batteries working.
2. A personal amplifier with headphones if there are no aids or they are not enough.
3. The right glasses on, reading or distance as the task needs.
4. Large print and good light, without glare.
5. A quiet room with the door closed.

Then write the adaptations next to the score: "aids in, amplifier used, large print". The next clinician can then read the number knowing how it was obtained, and repeat the test the same way.

Adaptations may not remove the effect of sensory loss on the score. Recording them is how the reader allows for that.

posts.title: Earwax: fixable, and harder to get treated
posts.insight: In England, NICE says wax removal belongs in primary care, but GP practices are not obliged to provide it unless locally commissioned, so access varies; in small care home studies wax was common and removal improved hearing in most blocked ears.
posts.angle: A simple treatment that improves hearing depends on local commissioning. People in care homes and people who can't travel or pay are the most exposed. Ask the practice where NHS wax removal is provided locally.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the commissioning position and care home findings are empirical and documentary; that this falls hardest on care home residents and people who can't pay is judgement.

captions.x:
Who removes your earwax in England depends on where you live.

NICE says wax removal should be done in primary care. GP practices are not obliged to provide it unless it is commissioned locally, so access varies from area to area.

It is often worth doing. Small studies in care homes found wax needing removal in more than half of residents, and hearing improved in most blocked ears after removal.

In our view, a simple fix for poor hearing should not depend on a postcode or the ability to pay. Ask your practice where NHS wax removal is provided locally.
captions.linkedin:
Who removes your earwax in England depends on where you live.

NICE guidance says wax removal should be done in primary care. But GP practices in England are not obliged to provide it as a core service unless it is commissioned locally. The result is that access varies from area to area. This is a question of how services are commissioned, not a failing of individual practices.

Why it deserves attention: in small studies in care homes, wax needing removal was found in more than half of residents. In one US study of new nursing home residents, hearing improved in 80% of ears that had been blocked by wax, against 3% of ears that had not. These were small studies, but the direction is consistent. Guidelines also say the ears of hearing aid users should be checked for wax, because wax can stop an aid working well.

The people most likely to go without are those who can't easily travel to a clinic, can't pay privately, or live in a care home.

Our view: a simple treatment that restores hearing should be reachable for everyone who needs it, including people who are housebound or in care homes.

If you or someone you care for has blocked ears, ask the GP practice one direct question: where is NHS wax removal provided in this area?

Sources in the first comment.

posts.title: Suspected active GCA: steroid now, confirm the diagnosis
posts.insight: European (EULAR) recommendations say high-dose glucocorticoid should start immediately in active giant cell arteritis, with the diagnosis confirmed by imaging or biopsy.
posts.angle: Two actions, both prompt: start treatment immediately and arrange confirmation. Position (judgement): arranging the scan or biopsy should not hold up the first dose.
posts.position_basis: mixed: the recommendation is guideline content (EULAR 2018 abstract); 'the tests should not hold up the first dose' is clinical judgement, marked as such.

captions.x:
In active giant cell arteritis, European recommendations say high-dose glucocorticoid should start immediately: prednisolone 40 to 60 mg a day.

The same recommendations say the diagnosis should be confirmed by imaging or biopsy.

Giant cell arteritis is inflammation of large arteries, including those of the head.

Two jobs, both prompt. Our view: organising the scan or biopsy should not hold up the first dose.
captions.linkedin:
In active giant cell arteritis (GCA), European recommendations say high-dose glucocorticoid should start immediately: prednisolone 40 to 60 mg a day.

The 2018 EULAR recommendations for large vessel vasculitis also say the diagnosis should be confirmed, by imaging or by biopsy.

GCA is inflammation of large arteries, including the arteries of the head, a condition seen in older people.

That gives two jobs, both prompt:

1. Start high-dose glucocorticoid immediately.
2. Arrange confirmation by imaging or biopsy.

The EULAR abstract does not set out the order in which these should happen when the diagnosis is still only suspected, and this post does not add time windows or doses for visual symptoms, which come from guidance not reviewed here.

Our view, as clinical judgement: in an older person with a convincing story, the logistics of the scan or biopsy should not hold up the first dose. Write down the reason for starting and the plan for confirmation in the same note.
